passage:
I'm Maya, and I was minding my little sister Aditi at the park. Aditi held the bucket tight. “Anjali can't play. Kabir is my best friend today.” Anjali stood at the edge of the sandpit with a thumb near her mouth. I couldn't tell whether Aditi wanted to be mean or just wanted to feel big.

Then an aunty on the bench called, “We need a shopkeeper, and everyone gets a turn.” Aditi looked at the bucket, then at Anjali. “You can be the shopkeeper,” she said, not smiling. Anjali ran over.

qa.q: What did Aditi say about Anjali?
qa.a: Aditi said, “Anjali can't play. Kabir is my best friend today.”

qa.q: What might Aditi have wanted when saying Anjali can't play?
qa.a: Aditi may have been feeling possessive of Kabir and wanted to feel big and proud, though Maya cannot be sure whether Aditi meant to be mean.

qa.q: How did the aunty on the bench change the moment?
qa.a: The aunty said they needed a shopkeeper and everyone gets a turn, giving Aditi a way to include Anjali without losing face.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel standing at the edge of the sandpit with a thumb near the mouth?
qa.a: Anjali probably felt shy and hurt, wanting to join but afraid of being turned away.

grounding: A young child declares that another child cannot play and that a different child is the best friend, and a grown-up gently teaches that everyone gets a turn.

passage:
Monday. In the sandpit Parul held the red bucket. “Kamal can't play. He's not my friend.” Kamal stood still with his spade.

Tuesday. The teacher brought a turn chart. “Everyone gets a turn with the red bucket, and everyone can be in the game.” Parul frowned at the chart.

Thursday. Parul dug a big hole and shouted, “Kamal! I need a digger!” Kamal ran over. Parul handed him the red bucket, and they carried sand together.

qa.q: What did Parul say to Kamal in the sandpit on Monday?
qa.a: Parul said, “Kamal can't play. He's not my friend.”

qa.q: Why might Parul have said Kamal can't play?
qa.a: Parul may have felt proud and powerful holding the red bucket, or wanted to test who gets to decide, as young children often explore power and closeness.

qa.q: What did the teacher bring that helped the class?
qa.a: The teacher brought a turn chart so everyone gets a turn with the red bucket and can be in the game.

qa.q: What might Kamal have felt standing still with the spade on Monday?
qa.a: Kamal probably felt left out and unsure, holding the spade and waiting.

grounding: Young children declare who can play, and over several days a teacher gently teaches that everyone gets a turn.

passage:
“Mahima is MY best friend,” Kavitha announced in the living room. “Tinku can't play kitchen with us.”
Tinku's lip wobbled. He held out his plastic cup.
“Why can't he?” asked Amma from the sofa.
“Because.” Kavitha put her arm around Mahima. “Only best friends.”
Mahima looked at Tinku, then at Kavitha, unsure.
Amma came and sat on the floor. “In our house, everyone gets a turn. Tinku can be the customer. You two can cook for him.”
Kavitha thought about it. “He has to say please.”
“Please,” said Tinku.
Kavitha poured him pretend tea. Mahima giggled.

qa.q: What game were Kavitha and Mahima playing?
qa.a: They were playing kitchen.

qa.q: How did Tinku feel when Kavitha said he couldn't play?
qa.a: He felt hurt and left out; his lip wobbled.

qa.q: How did Amma gently teach turns?
qa.a: She sat with them and gave Tinku a role, the customer, so everyone could play without scolding Kavitha.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt when Kavitha put an arm around her?
qa.a: Mahima seemed unsure, pleased to be chosen but uneasy about Tinku being left out.

grounding: Shows a young child declaring a best friend and excluding another, and an adult gently teaching that everyone gets a turn.

passage:
Nursery note, sand kitchen corner, Thursday.
Today Hansa stood at the edge of the sand kitchen with her arms out and told Arnab, “You can't play. You're not my friend today.” Arnab stood watching, holding his little bucket.
The two girls inside watched Hansa.
I sat down in the sand with them and said, “In our class, everyone gets a turn. Arnab can bring the water. Hansa, will you show him where it goes?” Hansa thought, then pointed. “There.” Soon they were cooking together. It seems to be about feeling in charge.

qa.q: What was Arnab holding?
qa.a: He was holding his little bucket.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she held her arms out?
qa.a: She seemed to be enjoying feeling powerful and in charge, deciding who could come in.

qa.q: Why was giving Hansa the job of showing Arnab a wise move?
qa.a: It let her keep feeling in charge while including Arnab, so the teacher taught turns without a fight.

qa.q: How might the two girls inside have felt?
qa.a: They seemed unsure, watching Hansa to see if they should follow her or not.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child declaring who can play and excluding a boy, and gently teaches that everyone gets a turn.

passage:
In Nani's village courtyard, the children played ring-a-roses under the neem tree.
“Ritvik can't play,” Kashish announced, holding hands with her cousins. “Only my team.”
Ritvik, the neighbour's small boy, stood by the water pump, twisting his shirt.
Nani, sorting lentils on the charpai, called out, “Kashish, come here.”
Kashish came, dragging her feet.
“When your cousins came from Delhi last summer, did they let you play?”
Kashish nodded slowly.
“Then here, everyone gets a turn in the circle.”
Kashish went back and held out her hand to Ritvik. He ran into the ring, beaming.

qa.q: Where was Ritvik standing?
qa.a: He was standing by the water pump.

qa.q: What was Ritvik feeling as he twisted his shirt?
qa.a: He was feeling left out and nervous, waiting to be allowed in.

qa.q: How did Nani help Kashish include Ritvik?
qa.a: She reminded Kashish of being included herself and said everyone gets a turn, so Kashish chose to hold out her hand.

qa.q: How might Kashish's cousins have felt when Ritvik joined?
qa.a: They were probably happy to have one more in the ring and followed Kashish's lead.

grounding: Shows a young child declaring who can play and excluding a neighbour, and a grandmother gently teaching that everyone gets a turn.

passage:
At the sandpit behind the nursery in Valencia, Alejandro spread his arms across the castle. "Only me and Esther. Esther's my best friend. Lucas can't play."
Lucas, holding a red bucket, stopped. Esther looked from one boy to the other.
Señora Ruiz crouched beside them. "In our sandpit, everyone gets a turn. Alejandro, what job could Lucas have?"
Alejandro thought hard. "He can... do the moat?"
Lucas's face lit up. He tipped his bucket of water, the moat flooded, and all three shrieked with laughter.

qa.q: What was Lucas holding?
qa.a: A red bucket.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro spread his arms across the castle?
qa.a: Alejandro felt possessive and a bit worried about sharing Esther, so he tried to control who could play.

qa.q: How did Señora Ruiz handle it gently?
qa.a: She stated the rule simply and asked Alejandro to find Lucas a job, so he chose to include Lucas himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Lucas when he was told he couldn't play?
qa.a: Lucas felt hurt and stuck, standing still with his bucket, then happy once he got the moat job.

grounding: Shows a young child declaring who can and cannot play, and an adult gently teaching that everyone gets a turn.
